analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance plans to cover mammograms and Pap smears for women.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in either chamber; it sat in two House subcommittees until the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every health insurance policy and every employer health plan to cover screening mammograms and Pap smears, with limits on extra charges and a set schedule for how often the tests must be covered. It applied to HMOs and employer plans, let states keep stricter rules of their own, and gave state regulators and the federal government tools to enforce it. It was introduced in June 1996, referred to two House committees, sent to subcommittees, and never came to a vote before Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.who_benefits: Women with health insurance would gain guaranteed coverage for mammograms and Pap smears with no worse cost-sharing than other similar services, catching breast and cervical cancers earlier. Radiology facilities and labs performing the tests would also gain volume of covered screening.

how_it_helps.text: Every health insurance policy and group health plan must include coverage for screening Pap smears and low-dose screening mammography [S2] [S3].

The bill sets a schedule: a baseline mammogram for women 35–40, annual mammograms for women 50 and older or judged at-risk, and at least every other year otherwise; Pap smears at least once a year or more if a physician recommends [S3].
Plans may not apply deductibles, coinsurance, or other limits to these tests that are worse than what they apply to similar services [S3].

The bill lets state rules stand wherever they give women greater protection, and charges state regulators with enforcing the requirements, with the Health and Human Services Secretary able to step in with penalties if a state will not [S2] [S3].
For employer plans governed by ERISA, the requirement is treated as part of that law so the usual enforcement tools apply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, HMOs, and employers sponsoring health plans would bear the cost of covering these screening tests for their enrollees and employees, likely passed into premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers with plans

drawbacks.text: A coverage mandate raises costs for insurers and self-insured employers, which typically show up as higher premiums for everyone with coverage, including people who do not use the screening [S3].

The bill sets fixed screening intervals (for example, mammograms at least every other year), which critics of screening mandates have argued can lock in one-size-fits-all rules instead of letting plans and doctors tailor frequency to individual risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — earlier detection of breast and cervical cancer through guaranteed, affordable screening — is real and targeted at a test most plans already partially covered. The main cost is higher premiums spread across all insured people, which is the normal trade-off of any coverage mandate. The design is reasonable: it defers to stronger state laws and builds in physician discretion for more frequent testing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, sent to health and workplace subcommittees in June and July 1996, and neither ever advanced it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jon Fox (R-PA) introduced the bill on June 12, 1996, joined by original cosponsors from both parties [S3].
It was referred to the Commerce Committee and the Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee the day it was introduced [S1] [S5].
Within a month it was sent to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations [S5].
No further action was recorded; it never reached a committee vote or the House floor before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, HMOs, and employers with health plans are better off because the mandate never became law and they never had to cover these screenings on the bill's terms.

for.name: Rep. Jon D. Fox
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring coverage of mammograms and Pap smears.

for.name: Reps. Gene Green, Lipinski, Roukema, Davis, and Forbes
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, making the bill bipartisan from the start.

against.name: House Commerce and Economic and Educational Opportunities Committees and their subcommittees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, sent it to subcommittees, and never advanced it to a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors and cosponsors came from both parties (2 Democrats and 6 Republicans among 8 cosponsors), and the bill died in committee without any recorded party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to cover mammograms and Pap smears with limited cost-sharing, adding to their claims costs. Because it never became law, their coverage practices remained their own choice.
Employer plans were covered too, so businesses would have paid for the added benefits through their plans, a cost they avoided when the bill died.
Guaranteed coverage of screening would have brought more patients whose tests were paid by insurance, a gain tied directly to women getting screened.
